PREDICT · EVERYONE COMMITS

Before I show you

An LED is connected to a 5 V pin with no resistor. What happens?

A

It lights, dimmer than usual

B

It lights, then burns out

C

Nothing: 5 V is too small

THE ANSWER

click to reveal

THE ANSWER

It lights — and then it burns out.

5 V pushes far more current through an LED than its junction can survive. The resistor is not there to dim it; it is there to set the current to about 15 mA.

Hands up for the one you chose — then we find out.

THE IDEA

A pin is a metal leg that code can switch

HIGH puts 5 V on it. LOW takes the 5 V away. There is no half-on.

The same pin, two states. The resistor stays the same in both.

Y7.1 · MAKE A LIGHT BLINK

7/180

DECODE THE CODE

Six lines, one blinking light

void setup() {

pinMode(13, OUTPUT);

}

void loop() {

digitalWrite(13, HIGH);

delay(500);

digitalWrite(13, LOW);

delay(500);

}

PINMODE(13, OUTPUT)

Faces pin 13 outwards. It will push current, not listen.

DIGITALWRITE(13, HIGH)

Connects pin 13 to 5 V. Current flows, the LED lights.

DELAY(500)

Waits 500 ms — half a second — doing nothing at all.

Type it. Do not copy it.

A button is wired to pin 2, and nothing else is on pin 2. The button is open. What does digitalRead(2) return?

LOW, because nothing is connected

B

HIGH, because nothing is connected

THE ANSWER

THE ANSWER

It changes at random.

A pin with nothing holding it is a tiny aerial. It picks up whatever is nearby — a hand, a cable, the mains — and flips between 0 and 1. That is called a floating pin.

THE IDEA

An input pin must be held at a known voltage

A resistor ties the pin to 0 V, so it stays LOW until the button pulls it up to 5 V.

10 kΩ is a weak hold: enough to fix the voltage, not enough to waste current.

Y7.2 · A BUTTON THAT LIGHTS A LAMP

19/180

DECODE THE CODE

Read it, then use it

void setup() {

pinMode(2, INPUT);

pinMode(13, OUTPUT);

Serial.begin(9600);

}

void loop() {

int pressed = digitalRead(2);

digitalWrite(13, pressed);

Serial.println(pressed);

delay(50);

}

PINMODE(2, INPUT)

Faces pin 2 inwards. It listens; it never pushes current out.

DIGITALREAD(2)

Answers one question: is pin 2 nearer 0 V or 5 V? HIGH or LOW.

DIGITALWRITE(13, PRESSED)

Whatever came in goes straight out. Press, and the LED is on.

Serial Monitor: the button at the bottom right.

Y7.3 · TWO THINGS MUST BE TRUE

31/180

DECODE THE CODE

One rule, two inputs

void setup() {

pinMode(2, INPUT);

pinMode(3, INPUT);

pinMode(13, OUTPUT);

}

void loop() {

int a = digitalRead(2);

int b = digitalRead(3);

if (a == HIGH && b == HIGH) {

digitalWrite(13, HIGH);

} else {

digitalWrite(13, LOW);

}

}

&&

Both sides true. One false side and the whole line is false.

||

Either side true is enough. False only when both are false.

ELSE

Runs when the if was false. One per if, at most.

Say the condition out loud before you run it.

THE IDEA

A variable lives where you put it

Declared outside loop(), the box survives. Declared inside, it is emptied every time round.

Where you write the line matters as much as what the line says.

Y7.4 · THE BOARD REMEMBERS

43/180

DECODE THE CODE

One line that keeps a number

int count = 0;

void setup() {

pinMode(2, INPUT);

Serial.begin(9600);

}

void loop() {

if (digitalRead(2) == HIGH) {

count = count + 1;

Serial.println(count);

delay(250);

}

}

INT COUNT = 0;

Made once, before setup runs. The value stays until you change it or unplug the board.

COUNT = COUNT + 1;

Read the old value, add one, put it back. The right-hand side is worked out first.

DELAY(250);

A crude debounce. Without it, one press is counted many times.

Try it with and without delay(250).

Remove delay(250). Store millis() each time you count, and only count again if 300 ms have passed. That is debouncing, and every real button needs it.

THE IDEA

A sequence of states is a machine

List the states. Then list what moves you from one to the next. That list is the program.

Each circle is a set of outputs. Each arrow is one delay and a change.

BUILD · 15 MINUTES

Y7.5 · DESIGN A CROSSING

55/180

DECODE THE CODE

Four states, in order

void setup() {

pinMode(9, OUTPUT); // green

pinMode(10, OUTPUT); // amber

pinMode(11, OUTPUT); // red

}

void loop() {

digitalWrite(9, HIGH); // green

delay(6000);

digitalWrite(9, LOW);

digitalWrite(10, HIGH); // amber

delay(2000);

digitalWrite(10, LOW);

digitalWrite(11, HIGH); // red

delay(6000);

digitalWrite(10, HIGH); // red + amber

delay(2000);

digitalWrite(11, LOW);

digitalWrite(10, LOW); // back to green

}

EVERY STATE SETS EVERY PIN

A pin stays where you left it. Switching one on is not switching the others off.

DELAY(6000)

Six seconds of doing nothing at all. Nothing else on the board runs during a delay.

ORDER MATTERS

The loop runs top to bottom, then starts again. The last line leads back to the first state.

Time one full cycle with a stopwatch.

Y7.5 · DESIGN A CROSSING

WATCH FOR

Why does a volume dial feel different from a light switch?

}

ANALOGREAD(A0)

A number from 0 to 1023. Not volts: a step number.

MAP(RAW, 0, 1023, 0, 100)

DECODE THE CODE

Sensor, rule, action

void setup() {

pinMode(9, OUTPUT);

Serial.begin(9600);

}

void loop() {

int light = analogRead(A0);

Serial.println(light);

if (light < 300) {

digitalWrite(9, HIGH);

} else {

digitalWrite(9, LOW);

}

}

INT LIGHT = ANALOGREAD(A0);

A snapshot, once per pass. It does not update by itself.

IF (LIGHT < 300)

The rule. Below 300 means darker, because the LDR is the top half.

DIGITALWRITE(9, HIGH)

The action. Sense, decide, act: that is the whole device.

Cover the sensor with your hand.

DECODE THE CODE

From a dial to a duty cycle

void setup() {

pinMode(6, OUTPUT);

Serial.begin(9600);

}

void loop() {

int knob = analogRead(A0);

int level = map(knob, 0, 1023, 0, 255);

analogWrite(6, level);

Serial.println(level);

delay(30);

}

ANALOGWRITE(6, LEVEL)

0 is off, 255 is fully on, and everything between is a duty cycle.

MAP(KNOB, 0, 1023, 0, 255)

analogRead has 1024 steps; analogWrite takes 256. map converts.

PIN 6

Only PWM pins can do this: 3, 5, 6, 9, 10 and 11 on an Uno.

0 to 255 is 256 values, not 255.

DECODE THE CODE

Three lines from a reading to a temperature

void setup() {

Serial.begin(9600);

}

void loop() {

int raw = analogRead(A0);

float volts = raw * 5.0 / 1024.0;

float celsius = (volts - 0.5) * 100.0;

Serial.print(celsius);

Serial.println(" C");

delay(500);

}

RAW * 5.0 / 1024.0

The reading as a voltage. The .0 matters: 5/1024 in whole numbers is 0.

(VOLTS - 0.5)

The sensor puts out 0.5 V at 0 °C. Subtract it so the scale starts at zero.

* 100.0

10 mV per degree is 0.01 V, so multiply by 100.

Print volts too while you debug.

Wire the plant alarm

Y8.5 · A PLANT ALARM THAT WILL NOT CHATTER

115/180

DECODE THE CODE

A flag, two rules, two outputs

int dry = 0;

void setup() {

pinMode(8, OUTPUT);

pinMode(9, OUTPUT);

Serial.begin(9600);

}

void loop() {

int wetness = analogRead(A0);

if (wetness < 380) dry = 1;

if (wetness > 420) dry = 0;

digitalWrite(8, dry);

digitalWrite(9, dry);

Serial.println(wetness);

delay(200);

}

IF (WETNESS < 380) DRY = 1;

One rule sets the flag. A variable that remembers a decision is a state.

IF (WETNESS > 420) DRY = 0;

A second rule clears it. Between the marks, nothing changes.

DIGITALWRITE(8, DRY)

The flag drives the output. The sensor never drives it directly.

Between 380 and 420, nothing happens.

A pin is a logic output, not a power output. 400 mA is twenty times its limit. The output inside the chip heats up, and the damage may not show until a later lesson.

B

click to reveal

To give the collapsing magnetic field a safe path.

A motor is a coil. Switch it off and the field collapses, and the coil generates a voltage spike that can destroy the transistor. The diode sends that current round the motor instead.

THE IDEA

The error is the difference between the target and the measurement. The controller acts on the error.

162/180

BUILD · 15 MINUTES

Give the arm two eyes

1

2

Each needs its own 10 kΩ to GND.

Y9.4 · A SYSTEM THAT CORRECTS ITSELF

163/180

DECODE THE CODE

The loop, in twelve lines

#include <Servo.h>

Servo arm;

int angle = 90;

void setup() {

arm.attach(9);

arm.write(angle);

Serial.begin(9600);

}

void loop() {

int left = analogRead(A0);

int right = analogRead(A1);

if (left > right + 40) angle = angle - 2;

if (right > left + 40) angle = angle + 2;

angle = constrain(angle, 0, 180);

arm.write(angle);

Serial.println(angle);

delay(20);

}

LEFT > RIGHT + 40

A deadband: a small difference is ignored, so the arm does not hunt.

ANGLE = ANGLE - 2

The correction. Small steps, often, beat one big jump.

CONSTRAIN(ANGLE, 0, 180)

Keeps the command inside the servo's travel.

Shade one LDR with your hand.

THE IDEA

Data needs a format

Label, value, separator, end of line. That is a protocol, and it is all you need.

T:23.5,L:512 and a newline. The newline is the end of the message.

BUILD · 15 MINUTES

Y9.5 · A DEVICE THAT REPORTS

175/180

DECODE THE CODE

Labels, values, and one newline

void setup() {

Serial.begin(9600);

}

void loop() {

int light = analogRead(A0);

float volts = light * 5.0 / 1024.0;

Serial.print("L:");

Serial.print(light);

Serial.print(",V:");

Serial.print(volts, 2);

Serial.println();

delay(1000);

}

PRINT VS PRINTLN

print adds nothing. println adds the newline that ends the message.

L: AND V:

Labels. The receiver knows which number is which without counting.

VOLTS, 2

Two decimal places. A format decision, not a measurement.

One line per second. Read it aloud.
